_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for Singapore covering Temasek/Singapura (Sang Nila Utama legend), Srivijaya/Majapahit, Portuguese raid 1613, Johor Sultanate, Stamford Raffles founding 1819, British Straits Settlements, WWII Japanese occupation (Sook Ching massacre), merger with Malaysia 1963, expulsion 1965, Lee Kuan Yew's authoritarian modernization, economic miracle (entrepot to high-tech), PAP dominance, and city-state governance.

religion.note: Secular state; religious harmony legally protected (Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act); Chinese majority Buddhist/Taoist; Malays constitutionally Muslim; Tamil Hindus; tolerance but sensitive to proselytization

ethnic_groups.name: Chinese
ethnic_groups.notes: Dominant; Hokkien, Teochew, Cantonese, Hainanese, Hakka dialect groups; Mandarin official (Speak Mandarin Campaign 1979); Chinese educated (Nanyang University closed) vs English-educated elite; prosperous middle class; PAP support base

ethnic_groups.name: Malay
ethnic_groups.notes: Indigenous; Singapore is in Malay archipelago; constitutionally special position (President must be Malay); Malay-Muslims; lower socioeconomic status; Geylang Serai; Group Representation Constituency (GRC) ensures representation

ethnic_groups.name: Indian
ethnic_groups.notes: Mostly Tamil (75% of Indians); also Malayali, Punjabi Sikhs, Gujarati; Little India; professionals and workers; historically brought by British

ethnic_groups.name: Other (Eurasian, Caucasian, etc.)
ethnic_groups.notes: Eurasian community (Portuguese-Asian mixed, Kristang creole); Western expats; Filipino domestic workers

independence.from: Expelled from Malaysia (was briefly part of Malaysia 1963-1965); British colony 1819-1963

country_profile.notes_unique: Only city-state in Southeast Asia; Lee Kuan Yew ruled 1959-1990 (authoritarian, meritocracy, anti-corruption); caning for vandalism (Michael Fay 1994); chewing gum ban; death penalty for drugs; PAP one-party dominance (since 1959, never lost power); from third world to first in one generation; Marina Bay Sands; Changi Airport (world's best); water self-sufficiency (NEWater); no natural resources (imports everything); ethnic quotas in HDB housing; 'Asian values'; financial hub

current_leader.name: Lawrence Wong
current_leader.title: Prime Minister
current_leader.notes: PAP; fourth-generation leader; economist; former Finance Minister; COVID-19 task force; succeeded Lee Hsien Loong

president.name: Tharman Shanmugaratnam
president.title: President
president.notes: First Indian-origin president elected by popular vote (ceremonial role); economist; former DPM; highly respected globally

former_prime_ministers.name: Lee Hsien Loong
former_prime_ministers.notes: Eldest son of Lee Kuan Yew; PAP; mathematician/general; cancer survivor; smart nation; family feud over Lee Kuan Yew's house (with siblings); wife Ho Ching (Temasek Holdings CEO)

former_prime_ministers.name: Goh Chok Tong
former_prime_ministers.notes: PAP; 'kinder, gentler' Singapore; financial crisis 1997; allowed more political openness; transitioned from LKY to LHL

former_prime_ministers.name: Lee Kuan Yew
former_prime_ministers.notes: Founding father; Cambridge-educated; authoritarian modernizer; 'Minister Mentor' until 2011; meritocracy, anti-corruption, multiracial, English-language policy; transformed fishing village to first world; died 2015 (state funeral); wife Kwa Geok Choo (lawyer)

910.name: Ancient Singapura and Temasek
910.description: Archaeological evidence of early settlement, the island's role as Temasek in maritime trade networks, Chinese and Indian references, and the legendary founding of Singapura.

sub_clusters.name: Early Trade Settlement
sub_clusters.description: Archaeological finds at Fort Canning Hill indicating early habitation, the island's position on maritime trade routes between India and China, and references in Ptolemy's Geographia.

sub_clusters.name: Temasek and the Singapura Legend
sub_clusters.description: The island known as Temasek ('Sea Town'), the legendary founding of Singapura by Sri Tri Buana (Sang Nila Utama) and the sighting of a lion, and its role as a minor trading port under Srivijayan influence.
key_events: Sang Nila Utama allegedly sights a lion and names the island Singapura ('Lion City') (c. 1299)

920.name: Singapura Kingdom and Malay Port
920.description: The Kingdom of Singapura under the Malay Annals, Majapahit and Siamese attacks, the port's destruction, and the island's obscurity during the Malacca and Johor Sultanate periods.

sub_clusters.name: Kingdom of Singapura
sub_clusters.description: The founding dynasty's five kings, Singapura as a trading port, the Majapahit attack, and the flight of the last king Parameswara who went on to found Malacca.
key_events: Parameswara flees Singapura after a Majapahit attack and later founds Malacca (c. 1398–1400)

sub_clusters.name: Obscurity Under the Johor Sultanate
sub_clusters.description: Singapore as a minor outpost of the Johor Sultanate, Portuguese burning of the settlement in 1613, and the island's descent into a sparsely populated backwater.

930.name: Founding of Modern Singapore
930.description: Stamford Raffles' founding of the British trading post, the rapid growth as a free port, immigration from China, India, and the Malay world, and the transfer to Crown Colony status.

sub_clusters.name: Raffles and the Free Port
sub_clusters.description: Sir Stamford Raffles' treaty with Sultan Hussein Shah and the Temenggong, the establishment of Singapore as a free trading port, the rapid influx of merchants, and the formation of the Straits Settlements.
key_events: Stamford Raffles establishes a British trading post at Singapore (6 February 1819)

sub_clusters.name: Straits Settlements Growth
sub_clusters.description: Singapore's rapid growth as entrepôt, mass Chinese and Indian immigration, the opium and pepper/gambier trades, the establishment of social institutions, and the transfer from the East India Company to Crown Colony status.
key_events: Singapore becomes a Crown Colony directly under the Colonial Office (1867)

940.name: Crown Colony and Rise as Entrepôt
940.description: Singapore's golden age as the premier entrepôt of Southeast Asia, the rubber and tin trade boom, the opening of the Suez Canal, the construction of the naval base, and the diverse colonial society.

sub_clusters.name: Entrepôt Golden Age
sub_clusters.description: The opening of the Suez Canal boosting trade, the rubber and tin boom, the growth of Chinese clan associations and Indian communities, and Singapore's position as the commercial hub of the Malay world.
key_events: Opening of the Suez Canal dramatically increases Singapore's trade volumes (1869)

sub_clusters.name: Naval Base and Pre-War Period
sub_clusters.description: The construction of the Singapore Naval Base as the 'Gibraltar of the East', inter-war economic fluctuations, the growth of local political consciousness, and the looming Japanese threat.

940.name: Fall of Singapore and Japanese Occupation
940.description: The catastrophic British defeat, the Japanese conquest renamed Syonan-to, the Sook Ching massacre, and the occupation's lasting impact on the local population's political consciousness.

sub_clusters.name: Fall of Singapore and Syonan-to
sub_clusters.description: The Japanese invasion down the Malay Peninsula, the fall of 'Fortress Singapore' — Churchill's 'worst disaster' — the Sook Ching massacre of Chinese civilians, and life under Japanese occupation.
key_events: Fall of Singapore — 80,000 British and Commonwealth troops surrender; Churchill calls it 'the worst disaster' in British military history (15 February 1942)
Sook Ching massacre — Japanese systematically screen and execute ethnic Chinese males (February–March 1942)

950.name: Post-War and Path to Self-Government
950.description: Post-war political awakening, the anti-colonial movement, the formation of the PAP under Lee Kuan Yew, self-government, and the merger with Malaysia.

sub_clusters.name: Anti-Colonial Politics
sub_clusters.description: Post-war political radicalization, communist-linked labor unrest, the Maria Hertogh riots, the founding of the People's Action Party, the Hock Lee Bus riots, and the achievement of self-government.
key_events: Lee Kuan Yew co-founds the People's Action Party (PAP) (1954)
Singapore achieves full internal self-government; Lee Kuan Yew becomes Prime Minister (1959)

sub_clusters.name: Merger with Malaysia
sub_clusters.description: The merger referendum, Operation Coldstore against left-wing opponents, Singapore's incorporation into the Federation of Malaysia, and the immediate political tensions.
key_events: Singapore joins the Federation of Malaysia (16 September 1963)

950.name: Separation and Early Independence
950.description: The traumatic separation from Malaysia, the existential crisis of independence, Lee Kuan Yew's nation-building, the withdrawal of British forces, and the foundations of Singapore's transformation.

sub_clusters.name: Separation and Survival
sub_clusters.description: The expulsion from Malaysia, Lee Kuan Yew's emotional press conference, the existential challenges of a small city-state without hinterland, the creation of national service, and the industrialization drive.
key_events: Singapore expelled from Malaysia and becomes an independent republic (9 August 1965)
Lee Kuan Yew weeps on national television announcing separation

sub_clusters.name: Early Nation-Building
sub_clusters.description: The withdrawal of British military forces, the Jurong industrial estate, the Housing Development Board's massive public housing program, bilingual education policy, and export-oriented industrialization.
key_events: British military withdrawal completed; Singapore accelerates self-reliance (1971)

960.name: Economic Miracle and Lee Kuan Yew Era
960.description: Singapore's transformation from Third World to First, the high-tech industrialization strategy, the development of Changi Airport and the Port of Singapore, and the consolidation of PAP dominance.

sub_clusters.name: High-Tech Industrialization and Development
sub_clusters.description: The shift to high-tech manufacturing, the creation of a world-class port and airport, the 'Second Industrial Revolution', the development of the financial sector, and Singapore's emergence as one of the Asian Tigers.
key_events: Changi Airport opens, becoming a global aviation hub (1981)
Singapore recognized as one of the Four Asian Tigers for its rapid economic growth

960.name: Mature City-State and Leadership Succession
960.description: The transition from Lee Kuan Yew to Goh Chok Tong and Lee Hsien Loong, the Asian financial crisis, the SARS outbreak, the integrated resorts, and Singapore's continued economic dynamism.

sub_clusters.name: Goh Chok Tong Era
sub_clusters.description: Goh Chok Tong's more consultative style, the 1997 Asian financial crisis, the SARS outbreak, and the transition of Singapore's economy toward knowledge-based industries.
key_events: SARS outbreak tests Singapore's public health systems (2003)

sub_clusters.name: Lee Hsien Loong Era
sub_clusters.description: Lee Hsien Loong's premiership, the opening of the integrated resorts (Marina Bay Sands), the 2011 watershed election, the death of Lee Kuan Yew, and the SG50 jubilee celebrations.
key_events: Marina Bay Sands integrated resort opens, transforming Singapore's skyline (2010)
Lee Kuan Yew dies — massive national outpouring of grief (23 March 2015)

960.name: Contemporary Singapore
960.description: Singapore in the 4G leadership transition, the COVID-19 response, the leadership transition to Lawrence Wong, smart nation initiatives, and the geopolitical balancing between the US and China.

sub_clusters.name: Fourth-Generation Leadership
sub_clusters.description: The 4G leadership succession process, the COVID-19 pandemic response and migrant worker dormitory crisis, the FICA foreign interference law, and Lawrence Wong's accession as Prime Minister in 2024.
key_events: COVID-19 exposes vulnerabilities in migrant worker dormitories (2020)
Lawrence Wong becomes Prime Minister, marking the 4G leadership transition (May 2024)

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
